function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run commands or push code directly, but I can walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take on your own machine (or in a CI job) to accomplish everything you listed.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re doing this inside a CI job, make sure the runner has SSH keys set up so it can pull from the private repo.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

Below is a quick “manual” analysis of what the repo contains and what we’ll generate.

| File | What it contains | What we’ll do |
|------|------------------|---------------|
| `package.json` | Node.js dependencies, scripts, start command | Use the `start` script as the entrypoint for Docker |
| `app.js` (or similar) | The actual Node.js app | Expose the port the app listens on (default 3000) |
| `README.md` | Documentation | No change needed |
| `Dockerfile` | *May or may not exist* | Create or update to use `node:18-alpine`, copy source, install deps, expose port, run `npm start` |
| `k8s/` | *May or may not exist* | Create a `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml` that reference the Docker image you’ll build |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | *May or may not exist* | Create a workflow that builds the Docker image, pushes it to a registry, and applies the k8s manifests |

### 2.1 Create / Update Dockerfile

If you want to use the helper function:

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "expose_port": 3000,
  "entrypoint": "npm start"
}
```

If you prefer to write it manually, here’s a minimal example:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

COPY . .

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why `node:18-alpine`?**  
> Alpine images are small and fast; Node 18 is the LTS version at the time of writing.

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML files

Using the helper function:

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "image_name": "ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 2,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "ClusterIP"
}
```

Manual example (`k8s/deployment.yaml`):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

And the service (`k8s/service.yaml`):

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **Note** – Adjust the image registry (`ghcr.io`, `docker.io`, etc.) to match where you’ll push.

### 2.3 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
      uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
      with:
        version: 'latest'
    - name: Deploy to K8s
      env:
        KUBECONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG_DATA }}
      run: |
        kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

> **What you’ll need**  
> * `KUBECONFIG_DATA` secret – Base64‑encoded kubeconfig for the cluster you’re deploying to.  
> * `GITHUB_TOKEN` is automatically available; it gives permission to push to GHCR.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you’re adding a new `k8s/` directory, you might need to create it first:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re running this inside a CI job** – you’ll need to configure a deploy key or PAT that has write access to the repo, then use `git config` to set the remote URL with credentials.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | `Dockerfile` exists & uses `node:18-alpine` |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` reference the correct image |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` builds & pushes the image, then applies the manifests |
| ✅ | All files are added, committed, and pushed |

Once you’ve pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger on the next push to `main`. It will build the image, push it to GHCR, and deploy it to your cluster.
